summary: Moon Base Mission is a free browser game and installable offline app for kids aged 7 to 12. Players run a Moon base for 10 days with four cat astronauts, balancing Power, Air & Water, Radiation Protection and Food. Every choice helps one system and hurts another, so there are no free choices, and a failed mission ends with a kind Mission Control debrief that explains the science and lets kids try again. Real NASA space-weather data (DONKI solar flares, solar clouds and particle events) sets the storm risk on the radiation days, and NASA photos illustrate the facts. Every data box is honestly labelled LIVE or ARCHIVED. It answers the challenge by teaching, in plain language, how life support, radiation shielding, power and food trade off on a lunar outpost. It matters because kids learn that survival in space is about smart trade-offs, not magic buttons.
details:
WHAT IT IS

Moon Base Mission is a free kids' game (ages 7 to 12) that works as a browser game and as an installable Android-style app. It is our answer to "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer". Kids become the commander of a Moon base with four cat astronauts (Capt. Space, Amy, Berry and Nikita) and must keep the base alive for 10 days, then launch before the 14-day Moon night begins.

HOW IT WORKS

Each day a new crisis appears, and the player must choose 1 of 3 options. There are no free choices: every option helps one thing and costs something else. The game has four equal base systems (Power, Air & Water, Radiation Protection, Food), plus Crew Mood and Science. After each choice there is an optional 10-second touch mini-game (10 different ones). Doing it well makes the choice work fully. Missing it halves the good effects, but the costs still apply. Each crew member has one special ability (Rally, Overclock, Deep Scan, Triage) that can be used once. At night the base uses up resources, so planning ahead matters. If any system reaches zero, the mission fails. On Day 10 the game checks whether the base is ready to launch and gives a Gold or Silver ending.

REAL NASA DATA

At game start the game fetches NASA DONKI space-weather data (solar flares, coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events) and photos from the NASA Image and Video Library. The class of a real solar flare sets the storm level on the radiation days (Day 3 and Day 8): C or none = level 1, M = level 2, X = level 3. Every data box is labelled LIVE (fetched now) or ARCHIVED (example data used when NASA does not respond within 8 seconds). The game never claims archived data is live.

LEARNING DESIGN

Every science card has two parts: "Real science" (what NASA knows) and "In the game (simplified)" (what we simplified). When a mission fails, kids see a kind Mission Control debrief that explains why in plain language and then get another try from a checkpoint (Day 4 or Day 7). Each day ends with a quick question.

MADE FOR KIDS

Big buttons, a rounded kid-friendly font, a Listen button that reads text aloud, Easy Mode for mini-games, calm background music with a mute control, stars, and 10 mission badges to collect. Progress is saved automatically in the browser, and the core mission works offline.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Kids learn why life support, radiation shielding, power and food have to be balanced on a real lunar outpost, and that space survival means smart trade-offs. Teachers and parents can use it free, with no account or install needed.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Motion animations, PWA (offline and installable). Built with Google AI Studio from our design and prompts. Intro and ending video clips were made with Google Gemini. The code includes about 27 automated tests for the game rules, audio rules and security rules.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Age-appropriate language, honesty about data (LIVE vs ARCHIVED), accuracy over spectacle, no features that need extra explanation, works on small phone screens, and fair costs so no choice is "always best".

LIMITS

Moon only, with simplified numbers. It has not yet been tested in a classroom. Next steps: a Mars version, a teacher mode, translations, and more NASA datasets.
